http://www.businessghana.com/site/news/g.text: +233(0)303-966-922 info@businessghana.com Contact Us Login Sign Up Home News General Cyber Security Authority, Czech Republic, ACDT partner to train journalists in cybercrime reporting Journalists and media practitioners across the country are to receive specialised training in cybercrime reporting as online fraud continues to affect both ordinary Ghanaians and senior public officials. The training forms part of the National Community Media Cyber Capability Building Project, which seeks to improve media coverage of cybercrime and strengthen public awareness of online safety. The project is being implemented by the Cyber Security Authority, the Africa Centre for Digital Transformation (ACDT) and the government of the Czech Republic under the Czech Republic's Transformation Cooperation Programme. Launching the project at the National Communications Authority Tower in Accra on Monday, August 3, 2026, the Deputy Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Mr Mohammed Adams Sukparu, said cyber security had become an important part of Ghana's digital development agenda. Representing the sector minister, Mr Samuel Nartey George, Mr Sukparu said cyber threats continued to evolve, making cyber security an economic, governance, national security and development issue. He said cyber fraud had become so widespread that even senior government officials were falling victim. Mr Sukparu disclosed that the Director-General of the Cyber Security Authority, Mr Divine Selase Agbeti, had informed him that two chief executives and a deputy minister were defrauded the previous week. He said the incident showed that no Ghanaian, regardless of position, was beyond the reach of cyber criminals. Mr Sukparu also recounted an experience during the 2024 general election campaign when he warned a family in his constituency that an offer of a vehicle from an overseas contact was fraudulent. He said the family ignored his advice, paid money to the fraudsters and later realised they had been deceived after losing the money. Addressing the gathering, Mr Agbeti said social engineering remained one of the hardest forms of cybercrime to combat because fraudsters often spent weeks or months studying their intended victims before making contact. He advised Ghanaians to be cautious about the personal information they shared on social media, explaining that details such as family members' names, schools attended and previous relationships were often used by fraudsters to gain the confidence of their targets. Mr Agbeti said the Cyber Security Authority worked with the Ghana Police Service, National Security, the Economic and Organised Crime Office and other security agencies to investigate cyber-enabled crime. He encouraged members of the public to report suspected online fraud through the Authority's 24-hour reporting line. A Board Representative of the Africa Center for Digital Transformation, Mr Emmanuel Agyare, said about 60 media houses would participate in the programme. He said the training would cover cyber security fundamentals, reporting on online fraud, digital forensics for journalists, media ethics, the law and child online protection, including sextortion. Mr Agyare said participants would be required to complete all training sessions and submit a journalistic report before being inducted into the proposed Cyber Security Press Corps, a national network of accredited journalists specialising in cyber security reporting. The Ambassador of the Czech Republic to Ghana, Mr Pavel Bílek, said the initiative built on more than four years of cooperation between Ghana and the Czech Republic in cyber security. He recalled that the Czech Republic donated specialised digital forensic hardware and software valued at almost GH¢450,000 to the Cybercrime Unit of the Ghana Police Service in May this year. Mr Bílek said more than 100 journalists and media practitioners would benefit directly from the programme, which would be held in Accra throughout August before moving to Kumasi in September. The Director of the National Counterterrorism Fusion Centre, Major General Dr Timothy Tifucro Ba-Taa-Banah, said violent extremist groups were increasingly using online platforms to recruit followers, raise funds and spread propaganda. He called for sustained engagement between the media and security agencies to improve public education on cyber threats. The President of the Private Newspaper and Online Publishers Association of Ghana, Mr David Sitsofe Tamakloe, urged journalists to verify information with credible sources and avoid publishing reports that could unintentionally spread fear. The Director of the KNUST E-Learning Centre, Professor Emmanuel Kofi Akowuah, said the university would support the project by helping to simplify cyber security concepts for journalists and the wider public.

https://www.hani.co.kr/arti/english_edit.text: Not even a war can stop Ukrainian kids from dreaming big with robotics Facebook 페이스북 Twitter 트위터 With the flip of a switch, a robot began to whir before setting off on its four wheels to find its target. After locating a box with the five sensors on all its sides and the bottom of its frame, the robot grabbed the box with its arms and put it down exactly where it was programmed to. The robot was created by Anna Tieliehina, a 14-year-old from Ukraine, who was responsible for everything from its design to its construction. “I made sure that the wheels were fastened tight so that the robot wouldn’t wobble when it picked up boxes,” Anna said when explaining how the robot was able to move with ease. Though war has raged on in Ukraine for over four years, the country’s children continue to dream big. Anna and Oles Letyta, 12, recently won a national robotics competition for children and teenagers in Ukraine, and were in Seoul to participate in the International Programming Robot Challenge, which took place on Sunday. The Hankyoreh met with Anna and Oles at the Ukrainian Embassy in Yongsan, Seoul, on Thursday to hear how robots helped them find their dreams. Anna’s robot specializes in pathfinding and carrying objects. It had the highest accuracy during the preliminary round, which involved finding a box in a maze and moving it to a specific destination. “We had to program the robot’s path at the competition venue. I quickly corrected the errors I found during the first round, so the robot did a better job navigating in the second round,” Anna said. Oles’ robot is a shooting robot controlled remotely via a joystick. The robot picked up a die and fired it forward, knocking the target away in a blink of an eye. Oles began making robots after his older brother went to Korea after winning the Ukrainian qualifiers last year. “To prepare for the competition, I would focus on designing my robot as soon as I was done with school and before dinner. I revised my first idea many times, so the whole process took about four months,” he said. Anna got her start in robotics after she began learning computer programming at school last year, when she was in seventh grade. Her teachers noticed her knack for the subject and introduced her to an outside professional instructor. From there, her coding skills improved by leaps and bounds. Her dedication was so strong that she spent hours after school practicing programming. Anna became the first female student to date to have won in the Ukrainian national qualifiers. Last year, not a single female student participated in the qualifiers, yet Anna went on to win first place in her very first robotics competition. “My mom was over the moon when she heard that I’d won. She’s cheering me on, saying that I’ll get even better results in the Korean competition,” Anna said with a smile. “My family said that representing your country isn’t an opportunity available to everyone, so they encouraged me to go to Korea and show off my skills,” Oles said. However, the ongoing war made concentrating on their robots far from easy for the young Ukrainians. Air raid sirens wail almost daily, warning of incoming missile and suicide-drone attacks and forcing the children to wake in the middle of the night and seek safety in underground shelters. “If the Shahed icon pops up on the air raid alert app, we run to the hallway. But if a missile icon pops up, our entire family has to run to the shelter,” said Oles. Since drones have only enough explosive power to destroy walls, people need only to seek shelter in hallways and away from windows. But ballistic missiles, which are powerful enough to topple entire buildings, force residents to flee underground for safety. Even in broad daylight, the children recounted seeing Russian drones flying through the streets. “I had missed the strike alert and was playing with my friends when a Shahed drone came flying by. It swerved at the last minute, flying above our heads before crashing into a nearby building,” Oles said, shaking his head as he recalled that close call. Even making the journey to Korea came with various complications, as Ukraine has closed its entire airspace to all commercial flights due to Russian strikes. The children had to travel by land to the neighboring country of Poland to board a plane to Beijing before finally arriving in Seoul. “The person screening luggage at the airport looked at our robots, which were from Ukraine, and asked if they were drones. We had to convince them that the robots didn’t fly or shoot bullets,” said Anna. Despite all the challenges they face, the children want to continue to make robots. “I want to become an engineer or a programmer to make programs for robots and applications that’ll help people in their daily lives,” Anna said. “First, I want to do well in this competition. Then, I’ll develop a new robot and enter a new contest. I’ll make a robot that’ll clean the streets of my home city, Lviv,” Oles said. The 12-year-old shared one last dream when we spoke with him. “I hope that the war doesn’t spread any further, so I can continue to study in Lviv,” he said. https://wowo.com/ivy-tech-to-host-career.text: Home Indiana News Ivy Tech to host career and college transfer expo in Warsaw (Photo supplied/Ivy Tech Community College) WARSAW, Ind. (WOWO) — Ivy Tech Community College’s Kosciusko County campus will host a career and college transfer expo Oct. 28, connecting attendees with employers and representatives from colleges and universities. The Web of Opportunities Transfer and Career Expo will run from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. at Ivy Tech’s campus, 2545 Silveus Crossing in Warsaw. Attendees can explore academic programs, learn about transfer options for four-year degrees, and connect with employers about jobs and internships. Participating employers include Lake City Bank, Flexaust, Slate Auto, Maple Leaf Farms, 3 Rivers, 80/20, Beyond Landscaping, OrthoWorx and Miller’s Merry Manor. Representatives from colleges and universities also are expected, including Ball State University, Butler University, Grace College, Indiana State University, Indiana Tech, Indiana University campuses, Manchester University, Purdue University Fort Wayne, the University of Saint Francis and Valparaiso University. The expo is open to people considering further education, looking for internships or exploring career opportunities.
